newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Salinas rejects murder cover up.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Salinas rejects murder cover up.

text.p: Former Mexican president Carlos Salinas has strongly denied interfering in a murder investigation to cover up his brother Raul's alleged involvement.

"Carlos Salinas de Gortari emphatically and firmly denies any insinuation that he may have intervened in the course of the investigation," the former president said in a statement sent to news media late on Thursday through his lawyer, Mariano Albor.

Prosecutors had presented new evidence this week suggesting Carlos Salinas knew his brother Raul was suspected of masterminding the 1994 shooting of a top ruling party politician but tried to get him off the hook.
Among that evidence was a cassette tape anonymously sent to prosecutors, in which one of a pair of brothers accused of helping in the murder said that Raul had ordered it.
Government opponents have raised doubts about the authenticity of the tape, but Attorney General Jorge Madrazo on Friday said there had been "absolutely no invention."
The Salinas family has always insisted that Raul, imprisoned in a maximum security jail since March 1995 on murder and illicit enrichment charges, is innocent.

Prosecutors believe Raul ordered the September 1994 murder of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, then secretary-general of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), because of a family feud. Ruiz Massieu was at the time divorced from Raul and Carlos's sister Adriana.

Carlos Salinas's statement said he hoped the investigation against his brother would be carried out "in accordance with the judicial responsibilities and the fundamental criteria of transparency and independence that society demands".
Enormously popular during his 1988-94 administration, Carlos Salinas fled Mexico shortly after Raul's arrest and currently lives in Dublin, Ireland.
Prosecutors visited Salinas in January to question him about Ruiz Massieu's murder.

His testimony was initially kept secret but on Wednesday the Attorney-General's office said Carlos Salinas had admitted to investigators being informed that Raul's name had come up during the inquiries into Ruiz Massieu's assassination.
He insisted, however, that he had given the man leading the investigation at the time, Ruiz Massieu's brother Mario, full freedom and independence to act according to the law.

Mario Ruiz Massieu is currently under house arrest in the United States pending repeated attempts by the Mexican government to have him extradited to face charges of obstructing justice and embezzlement.

Former Attorney-General Victor Humberto Benitez -- excluded from the murder investigation by Salinas -- gave a very different story to prosecutors about the president's involvement in the murder investigation.

He testified that he had been summoned to the official residence Los Pinos by Carlos Salinas after the murder. On arrival, he was shown into a small side room where Raul was waiting for him. Raul "expressed his concern that he was going to be involved in the investigation", Benitez said.
